Upon Mahalath--either an instrument, as a lute, to be used as an accompaniment (Leannoth, "for singing") or, as others think, an enigmatic title (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1">Psa 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">Psa 45:1</reference>, titles), denoting the subject--that is, "sickness or disease, for humbling," the idea of spiritual maladies being often represented by disease (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">22:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.15">15</reference>, &c.). On the other terms, see on <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>. Heman and Ethan (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.89.1">Psa 89:1</reference>, title) were David's singers (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.18">1Ch 6:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.17">15:17</reference>), of the family of Kohath. If the persons alluded to (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.31">1Ki 4:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.6">1Ch 2:6</reference>), they were probably adopted into the tribe of Judah. Though called a song, which usually implies joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.1">Psa 83:1</reference>), both the style and matter of the Psalm are very despondent; yet the appeals to God evince faith, and we may suppose that the word "song" might be extended to such compositions.</title> <div sID="gen9981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6511"/>1-2. Compare on the terms used, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.2">Psa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">31:2</reference>. <div eID="gen9981" type="x-p"/>
